title: Abandoned Infants and Food Fights: How Climate Extremes Are Breaking Monkey Societies
summary: For more than three decades, researchers at Lomas Barbudal in Costa Rica have studied white-faced capuchin monkeys, building one of the most detailed portraits of primate social life in the wild. Under normal conditions, capuchin mothers are fiercely devoted. But during the abnormally severe drought of 2015, driven by El Niño, evolutionary anthropologist Susan Perry witnessed something that seemed impossible: mothers ignoring their infants' desperate cries and simply walking away. 'Now, I was seeing babies crying on the ground piteously. And the mothers just looking down like 'Too much trouble' and walking off, abandoning their infants,' Perry said. It was a stark reminder that even the most resilient animals have breaking points. A new study published in Nature Ecology and Evolution, led by behavioral ecologist Odd Jacobson, set out to understand how climate variability reshapes capuchin societies. The team analyzed 33 years of geolocation data from 12 monkey groups, tracking daily fruit intake, home range size, and travel distances. They then used a hierarchical social relations model to predict how groups would interact and how their territories would overlap under different climate conditions. The findings upend some long-held assumptions. Typically, larger groups dominate smaller ones, seizing resource-rich areas like riverbanks during dry seasons. But during extreme climate events—whether unusually dry or wet—that advantage evaporates. 'We don't really know exactly why,' Jacobson said. 'Maybe there's not as much heterogeneity in the landscape during these resource poor times, and so there's not much that larger groups can monopolize.' At the same time, competition within groups intensifies, making foraging less efficient for everyone. The research suggests that climate extremes are disrupting the delicate balance that determines optimal group size. As global warming makes El Niño and La Niña events more intense, these disruptions could become the new normal. Filippo Aureli, an ethologist who studied the same drought's impact on spider monkeys, noted that capuchin infant mortality spiked, while spider monkeys simply stopped reproducing. 'With climate change, [these extremes] are going to be more frequent and intense,' Aureli said. 'And we don't know what's going to happen.' Perry emphasized the value of long-term data: 'We know what normal is. If you just try to drop in right now in all the chaos that we're starting to feel around the planet, then you really can't study it.' The study is a sobering glimpse into a future where even the most adaptable creatures may struggle to cope.
why_it_matters: The study is a window into a future where even the most adaptable creatures are pushed past their breaking point. For a young person, it shows that climate disruption isn't just about melting ice caps—it unravels the social fabric of whole societies, including those of our closest animal relatives.

background_read: White‑faced capuchin monkeys are highly intelligent New World primates known for complex social behaviors, including tool use and cooperative care of young.
Lomas Barbudal Biological Reserve in Costa Rica protects a tropical dry forest that experiences a strong wet‑dry cycle, making it an ideal natural laboratory to study how climate shapes animal lives.
El Niño is a Pacific Ocean climate pattern that warms ocean temperatures and disrupts weather globally; in Central America it often causes severe droughts that shrink fruit availability.
Susan Perry (an evolutionary anthropologist) began studying the Lomas Barbudal capuchins in the early 1990s, building one of the longest‑running primate field studies in the world.

The journal Nature Ecology & Evolution publishes top‑tier research; the study by Odd Jacobson’s team used 33 years of location data and a sophisticated model to predict how monkey groups’ territories overlap under stress.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A new study on white‑faced capuchins shows climate extremes can break even the most devoted monkey societies.
└─ SHOCKING ANOMALY: During the 2015 drought, mothers ignored crying infants and walked away—behavior scientists had never seen before.
SETTING: Lomas Barbudal, Costa Rica; researchers have tracked 12 monkey groups for 33 years, gathering detailed data on diet, travel, and home ranges.
TRIGGER: An abnormally severe drought, driven by El Niño, shattered normal resource availability.
STUDY METHOD: Behavioral ecologist Odd Jacobson and his team analyzed geolocation records and daily fruit intake, then built a hierarchical social relations model to simulate group interactions.
├─ Under normal conditions, larger groups dominate smaller ones and monopolize resource‑rich zones like riverbanks.
├─ During extreme dry or wet spells, that size advantage evaporates—possibly because the landscape becomes more uniform.
└─ Competition within groups also intensifies, making foraging less efficient for everyone.
BROADER IMPACT: As climate change makes El Niño and La Niña more intense, these social disruptions could become the new normal.
└─ OTHER SPECIES: Spider monkeys stopped reproducing; capuchin infant mortality spiked.
VALUE OF LONG‑TERM DATA: Perry explains that without decades of 'normal' to compare against, scientists cannot really understand the chaos that is spreading.

perspectives.description: Decades of patient fieldwork finally paid off: the researchers could detect a shocking behavioral shift only because they knew exactly what was normal. This underscores why we must invest in long‑term ecological monitoring even when results aren't immediate.

The findings are grim. If a species as intelligent and flexible as capuchins abandons its infants when stressed, less adaptable species might vanish entirely. It paints a bleak picture of a world where climate chaos unravels the bonds that hold animal societies together.

The research challenges old assumptions about group size and dominance. It reveals that the 'optimal' group structure is not fixed but depends heavily on environmental stability—a pattern that may apply to many social animals, forcing scientists to rethink basic models.

If extreme weather becomes routine, conservation strategies will need to change. Rather than protecting small isolated parcels, planners might focus on larger, more diverse landscapes that can buffer against climate shocks, or even explore assisted migration to help species find stable habitats.
